accuracy.evidence: Matches the National Curriculum for England Year 3 statement 'count from 0 in multiples of 4, 8, 50 and 100; find 10 or 100 more or less than a given number'. Every count in the lab, the sorter cards and the items was checked: 48 is 12 fours and 6 eights, 500 is 10 fifties, 130 to 930 is 8 hops of 100, 20 is a multiple of 4 but not 8, 680 + 100 = 780. The 1-to-40 grid marks exactly the ten multiples of 4 as a subset of the twenty even numbers.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets losing the jump size (sliding back to 2s or 10s: 16, 18, 20), counting the numbers said instead of the jumps, believing the 8s count needs more jumps than the 4s count, thinking every even number is a multiple of 4, and rounding when adding 100 (350 + 100 = 400 or 360). The adult notes name each; the Challenge why() tags two, one, four, ten, fifty, hund, round and both give a matching message.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagfours is a frog-on-a-number-line skip counter with tap-ahead hopping, a 1-to-40 multiples grid where the 2s are dotted and only the 4s may be tapped, a side-by-side race of a 4s frog and an 8s frog to 48, a 0-to-500 track in 50s and a 30-to-1030 track counting on in 100s. No other lab in learn/ counts in steps of 4, 8, 50 or 100 on a track, and the shingle check passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step makes the child produce the count themselves, one hop at a time, with the running list and the hop total shown under the track. Tasks finish only at the target (48, all ten 4s, both frogs at 48, 500, 930), and the done message states the fact learned: 12 hops of 4 equals 6 hops of 8, every second 2s number is a 4s number, two 50s make 100, only the hundreds digit changes.

predictions.evidence: Five predictions lock before the action: will you say 30 when counting in 4s (no: 28 + 4 = 32), is every 4s number also in the 2s count, how many hops of 8 reach 48 (6, versus the tempting 12), which number comes after 200 in the 50s count (250 versus 205 or 225) and what is 100 more than 350 (450 versus 400 or 360). Each result line restates the prediction and whether it was right.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven Challenge questions mix 4s, 8s, 50s and 100s, including 'what comes next 4, 8, 12, 16' with 17 (a jump of 1) and 18 (a jump of 2) as distractors and 100 more than 350 with 400 and 360. Wrong answers get a specific why() message tied to the tagged slip rather than a generic try again, and the right answer explains the jump.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs score Flesch-Kincaid grade 1.2 or below with short sentences built around the words jump, count and hop; adult paragraphs average about grade 4.4. Lab step text stays under three sentences, buttons use plain labels like +4, Mark next 4s number and 100 more, and numbers are written as digits so early readers can follow.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph carries a fact or a method: the jump size, the 2s to 4s to 8s doubling link, the half-as-many-jumps idea, the 50 and 00 pattern, and hundreds-digit change. The family tip gives concrete counting of legs (4 for a chair or cat, 8 for a spider) and house or bus numbers in 100s, with no padding or praise text.

mobile.evidence: Walked on iPhone 13 by walk.cjs in light and dark themes: tracks fit the width with labels every 4, 8, 100 or 100 from 30 still legible, the grid cells are tap-sized, controls stay on one row, and Show me finished each task inside six seconds. Hops can be made by tapping ahead of the frog on the track as well as with the buttons.

accessibility.evidence: axe reported no violations in either theme. The canvas has an aria-label and a live text summary listing the numbers said and the hop count, the grid marks the 2s with a dot as well as colour, wrong grid taps are explained in words, and all controls are real buttons reachable by keyboard.
